Chapter 1 · Foundations: diffusion, eigenmodes and the Bloch–Torrey equation

© 2026 Chantal Tax. All rights reserved. Shared for viewing only; not licensed for reuse or redistribution. Course: simulating the diffusion MRI signal. This chapter sets up the equations that every later method solves. What you'll take away
  1. How a pore's shape enters diffusion: through the eigenmodes of the Laplacian with the right interface conditions.
  2. How to derive those modes yourself for a slab, and where to look them up for cylinders and spheres.
  3. What the distribution of displacements looks like in a pore: its time-dependent diffusivity ||(D(t)||) and kurtosis ||(K(t)||).
  4. The Bloch–Torrey equation for the magnetization, and the signal as the average phase factor of random walkers.
  5. The full problem that every simulator solves (compartments, membranes, relaxation), and the simplifications behind the exact methods.
  6. The weak form of the same problem, and why choosing its test functions amounts to choosing a numerical method.
  7. Why the PDE and the random walk give the same signal (the Feynman–Kac relation), and what that means for simulation.
Every exercise has hints and a worked answer, folded away. Try the exercise first, then open the hint, then the answer.

1a · Diffusion and the eigenmodes of a pore

The diffusion equation

Let ||(C(\mathbf r,t)||) be the concentration of tagged water molecules (for us, later: magnetization). Two ingredients give the diffusion equation:
  1. Conservation. Molecules are not created or destroyed. What leaves a small volume must flow out through its surface.
  2. Fick's law. The flux points downhill, from high to low concentration: ||(\mathbf J = -D\nabla C||).
Together they give ||[\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = D\,\nabla^2 C .||]Fick (1855) proposed the flux law by analogy with Fourier's law of heat conduction (Fourier 1822): the same equation describes heat, with temperature for ||(C||) and conductivity for ||(D||).

data.text/html: ⇒ Take any fixed volume ||(V||) with surface ||(S||) and outward normal ||(\mathbf n||). The amount inside changes only by flow through the surface: ||[ rac{d}{dt}\int_V C\,dV = -\oint_S \mathbf J\cdot\mathbf n\,dS .||]⇒ The divergence theorem turns the surface integral into a volume integral: ||(\oint_S \mathbf J\cdot\mathbf n\,dS = \int_V abla\cdot\mathbf J\,dV||). ⇒ This holds for every volume ||(V||), so the integrands must be equal: ||(\partial C/\partial t = - abla\cdot\mathbf J||). ⇒ Insert Fick's law: ||(\partial C/\partial t = abla\cdot(D abla C)||). For uniform ||(D||) this is ||(D abla^2 C||). → Keep the form ||( abla\cdot(D abla C)||) in mind: it is the one to use when ||(D||) differs between compartments.

data.text/markdown:
The domain: pores, compartments and the voxel

The equation alone does not fix the solution. We also need where the molecules start, and what happens where they meet a wall. This is where the microstructure enters the problem. First some names (panel b follows the usual multi-compartment notation):
  • The domain ||(\Omega||) is the region the molecules live in: one closed pore (panel a), or the whole imaging voxel (panel b).
  • The voxel is split into compartments ||(\Omega_n||): the cells and the extracellular space ||(\Omega_e||).
  • Two compartments meet at an interface ||(\Gamma_{nm}||): a cell membrane.
  • The boundary ||(\partial\Omega||) is the outer edge of the voxel. Where a cell is cut by the voxel edge, that piece of its surface is called ||(\Gamma_n||).
So we have interface conditions (on membranes and cell walls: physics) and boundary conditions (on the voxel edge: a modelling choice about what lies outside the voxel). For a single closed pore the two coincide: its wall is an impermeable interface and also the edge of the domain.

Initial, interface and boundary conditions

Initial condition. Before the experiment the spins are in equilibrium and spread evenly: ||(C(\mathbf r,0)=\rho||), a constant (or one constant per compartment). Interface conditions on cell walls and membranes ||(\Gamma_{nm}||) (||(\partial/\partial n||): derivative along the outward normal):
Interface Condition What it means In a random walk
Impermeable, inert ||(\dfrac{\partial C}{\partial n}=0||) (Neumann type) no flux through the wall the walker is reflected
Permeable membrane ||(D_n\dfrac{\partial C_n}{\partial n_n} = -D_m\dfrac{\partial C_m}{\partial n_m} = \kappa\,(C_m - C_n)||) (transmission) the flux is continuous; the jump in ||(C||) across the membrane is set by the permeability ||(\kappa||) the walker crosses with a small probability, else it is reflected
Relaxing wall ||(D\dfrac{\partial C}{\partial n} + \varrho\, C = 0||) (Robin type) the wall destroys magnetization at a rate set by the relaxivity ||(\varrho||) the walker is removed with a small probability; rarely needed in soft tissue
Perfect sink ||(C = 0||) (Dirichlet type) every molecule that touches the wall is lost not realistic for dMRI
Two limits of the permeable membrane are worth remembering: ||(\kappa = 0||) gives an impermeable wall on both sides, and ||(\kappa\to\infty||) forces ||(C_n = C_m||), as if the membrane were not there. Boundary conditions on the voxel edge ||(\partial\Omega||):
Boundary Condition When to use it
Reflecting ||(\partial C/\partial n = 0||) the voxel is closed, or what lies outside does not matter
Periodic values and fluxes on opposite faces match; with a gradient on, up to a phase ||(e^{i\theta(t)}||), ||(\theta = \gamma g L\int_0^t f\,dt'||) the voxel is one tile of a repeating tissue; avoids artificial walls at the voxel edge
The names Neumann, Robin and Dirichlet refer to the type of condition (on the derivative, on a mix, on the value), wherever it is applied.

data.text/markdown:
The full problem, and the step to one compartment

Put the pieces together. In every compartment the molecules diffuse with their own diffusivity, starting from their own equilibrium density: ||[\frac{\partial C_n}{\partial t} = \nabla\cdot(D_n\nabla C_n)\ \text{ in }\Omega_n,\qquad C_n(\mathbf r,0) = \rho_n,||]with a reflecting voxel edge, ||(D_n\,\partial C_n/\partial n = 0||) on ||(\Gamma_n||), and on every membrane ||(\Gamma_{nm}||) ||[D_n\frac{\partial C_n}{\partial n_n} = -D_m\frac{\partial C_m}{\partial n_m} = \kappa_{nm}\big(c_{nm}C_m - c_{mn}C_n\big),\qquad c_{nm} = \frac{2\rho_n}{\rho_n + \rho_m} .||]→ Why the factors ||(c_{nm}||)? Compartments can hold different amounts of water at equilibrium, ||(\rho_n\ne\rho_m||). The plain condition ||(\kappa(C_m - C_n)||) would then drive a flux even at equilibrium and slowly even out the two densities, which real tissue does not do. The factors make the equilibrium state, ||(C_n = \rho_n||) in every compartment, a state without flux: ||(c_{nm}\rho_m - c_{mn}\rho_n = 0||) (check it). For equal densities ||(c_{nm} = 1||), and the condition is the one in the table. → The step to one compartment. Most of this chapter, and Chapters 2 and 3, work with a single pore: uniform ||(D||), reflecting walls, ||(\rho = 1||). That is the full problem with every interface made impermeable: each compartment then evolves on its own, and the voxel is a weighted sum of single pores. Membranes come back where they are the point: the exchange mode below (Exercise 9), exchange in Chapter 3, and the simulators of Chapters 4 and 5, which solve the full problem.

Eigenmodes: the natural patterns of a pore

Put the diffusion equation in a closed pore ||(\Omega||) with reflecting walls. Some concentration patterns keep their shape and only fade in amplitude. These are the eigenmodes ||(u_n(\mathbf r)||) of the pore. Any initial concentration can be written as a sum of eigenmodes, and each one fades at its own rate: ||[C(\mathbf r,t) = \sum_n c_n\, u_n(\mathbf r)\, e^{-D\lambda_n t}, \qquad -\nabla^2 u_n = \lambda_n u_n \ \text{in } \Omega, \qquad \frac{\partial u_n}{\partial n}=0 \ \text{on the walls.}||]
  • ||(\lambda_0 = 0||) with ||(u_0||) constant: the uniform state. It never fades, because reflecting walls conserve the total amount.
  • Every other mode fades with time constant ||(\tau_n = 1/(D\lambda_n)||). Finer patterns have larger ||(\lambda_n||) and fade faster.
  • The geometry enters only through ||(\lambda_n||) and ||(u_n||). Once you have them, you have solved diffusion in that pore for every starting condition and every time.
  • Separation of variables and expansion in modes go back to Fourier (1822); the general theory of such eigenproblems is Sturm–Liouville theory (Sturm 1836; Liouville 1836). In diffusion NMR, Robertson (1966) was the first to expand the magnetization in the modes of a slab.

data.text/html: ⇒ Try a product. Guess ||(C(\mathbf r,t)=u(\mathbf r)\,T(t)||) and put it in ||(\partial C/\partial t = D\nabla^2 C||): ||[u\,T' = D\,T\,\nabla^2 u .||]⇒ Separate. Divide by ||(D\,u\,T||): ||[\frac{T'}{D\,T} = \frac{\nabla^2 u}{u}.||]The left side depends only on ||(t||), the right only on ||(\mathbf r||). Both must equal the same constant; call it ||(-\lambda||). ⇒ Time part: ||(T' = -D\lambda T||), so ||(T(t) = e^{-D\lambda t}||). ⇒ Space part: ||(-\nabla^2 u = \lambda u||), with the wall condition ||(\partial u/\partial n = 0||) (it is a condition on ||(C||), so on ||(u||)). Only special values ||(\lambda_n||) allow a solution: the eigenvalues. ⇒ Superpose. The equation is linear, so any sum of such products is again a solution. The eigenmodes are orthonormal, ||(\int_\Omega u_m u_n\,d\mathbf r = \delta_{mn}||), so the coefficients follow from the initial condition by projection: ||[c_n = \int_\Omega u_n(\mathbf r)\,C(\mathbf r,0)\,d\mathbf r .||]⇒ Point source. Start with one molecule at ||(\mathbf r_0||): ||(C(\mathbf r,0) = \delta(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0)||). Then ||(c_n = u_n(\mathbf r_0)||), and the solution is the propagator, the probability density of being at ||(\mathbf r||) at time ||(t||) after starting at ||(\mathbf r_0||): ||[P(\mathbf r\mid\mathbf r_0,t) = \sum_n u_n(\mathbf r)\,u_n(\mathbf r_0)\,e^{-D\lambda_n t}.||]→ Why a point source if spins start everywhere? Because every other start is a sum of point sources: ||(C(\mathbf r,t) = \int P(\mathbf r|\mathbf r_0,t)\,C(\mathbf r_0,0)\,d\mathbf r_0||). One propagator serves all initial conditions.

(Quicker: multiply ||(-u''=\lambda u||) by ||(u||) and integrate by parts with the wall conditions: ||(\lambda\int u^2 = \int u'^2 \ge 0||).) ⇒ ||(\lambda = 0||): ||(u = A + Bx||), and ||(u' = B = 0||). So ||(u_0||) is a constant: the uniform mode. ⇒ ||(\lambda = k^2 > 0||): ||(u = A\cos kx + B\sin kx||). ||(u'(0) = Bk = 0||) gives ||(B = 0||). ||(u'(L) = -Ak\sin kL = 0||) with ||(A \ne 0||) needs ||(\sin kL = 0||), so ||(kL = n\pi||). ||[\lambda_n = \left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2,\qquad u_n(x) \propto \cos\frac{n\pi x}{L},\qquad n = 0,1,2,\dots||](b) ⇒ ||(\int_0^L A^2\cos^2(n\pi x/L)\,dx = A^2 L/2||) for ||(n \ge 1||), and ||(A^2 L||) for ||(n=0||). The slowest mode that still carries information fades with ||(\tau_1 = L^2/(\pi^2 D)||): 3.2 ms for ||(L = 8||) µm and ||(D = 2||) µm²/ms.

(a) ⇒ Mode ||(n||) still matters while ||(e^{-D\lambda_n t}||) is not negligible, say ||(D\lambda_n t \lesssim 5||) (||(e^{-5} < 1\%||)). ⇒ With ||(\lambda_n = (n\pi/L)^2||): ||(n \lesssim \dfrac{L}{\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{Dt}}||). ⇒ ||(t = 0.1||) ms: ||(n \approx \frac{10}{\pi}\sqrt{25} \approx 16||). ||(\ t = 10||) ms: ||(n \approx \frac{10}{\pi}\sqrt{0.25} \approx 2||). (b) The free Gaussian of Exercise 1, centred at ||(x_0||), as long as ||(\sqrt{2Dt}||) is small compared with the distance from ||(x_0||) to the nearest wall. Move ||(x_0||) close to a wall and you see the reflected part appear first there. (c) At long times only a handful of modes survive, so eigenmode methods are cheap exactly where diffusion has explored the whole pore. At short times you need many modes to build a narrow peak. There, a free Gaussian (or a random walk) is the natural description. You will see this trade-off again in Chapters 2 and 5.

Using the propagator, show that the mean-squared displacement is\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||[\\langle (x - x_0)^2\\rangle(t) = \\frac{L^2}{6} - \\frac{16L^2}{\\pi^4}\\sum_{n\\ \\text{odd}}\\frac{e^{-D(n\\pi/L)^2 t}}{n^4},||]\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003eand that it tends to \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(L^2/6||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e at long times. (In the random-walk notebook the walkers between two walls levelled off at \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(L^2/6||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. Here is where that number comes from.)\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

• Expand the square: ||(\langle(x-x_0)^2\rangle = \langle x^2\rangle + \langle x_0^2\rangle - 2\langle x\,x_0\rangle||).
  • Uniform start and reflecting walls mean the walkers stay uniform at all times, so ||(\langle x^2\rangle = \langle x_0^2\rangle = L^2/3||).
  • ||(\langle x\,x_0\rangle = \frac1L\iint x\,x_0\,P(x|x_0,t)\,dx\,dx_0||). Insert the mode sum: each mode contributes ||(\frac1L\big(\int_0^L x\,u_n\,dx\big)^2 e^{-D\lambda_n t}||).

⇒ ||(\langle x^2\rangle = \langle x_0^2\rangle = \frac1L\int_0^L x^2dx = \frac{L^2}{3}||). ⇒ ||(\langle x\,x_0\rangle = \frac1L\sum_n e^{-D\lambda_n t}\left(\int_0^L x\,u_n(x)\,dx\right)^2||). ⇒ ||(n=0||): ||(\int_0^L x/\sqrt L\,dx = L^{3/2}/2||), giving ||(\frac1L\cdot\frac{L^3}{4} = \frac{L^2}{4}||). ⇒ ||(n\ge1||): integrate by parts, ||(\int_0^L x\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}dx = \frac{L^2}{(n\pi)^2}\big[(-1)^n - 1\big]||). This is zero for even ||(n||) and ||(-2L^2/(n\pi)^2||) for odd ||(n||). With the factor ||(\sqrt{2/L}||) squared: ||(\frac1L\cdot\frac2L\cdot\frac{4L^4}{(n\pi)^4} = \frac{8L^2}{(n\pi)^4}||). ⇒ Put together: ||[\langle(x-x_0)^2\rangle = \frac{2L^2}{3} - 2\left[\frac{L^2}{4} + \sum_{n\ \text{odd}}\frac{8L^2}{(n\pi)^4}e^{-D\lambda_n t}\right] = \frac{L^2}{6} - \frac{16L^2}{\pi^4}\sum_{n\ \text{odd}}\frac{e^{-D\lambda_n t}}{n^4}.||]→ Check ||(t=0||): ||(\sum_{n\ \text{odd}} n^{-4} = \pi^4/96||), so the MSD is ||(L^2/6 - L^2/6 = 0||). ✓ → ||(t\to\infty||): all exponentials vanish and the MSD is ||(L^2/6||): start and end positions have become independent, each uniform in the slab. → The weights ||(8L^2/(n\pi)^4||) fall as ||(n^{-4}||): the first mode carries 98.6% of the total. Remember this. Exercise 5 shows where they come from, and in Chapter 2b the same weights set the signal in the Gaussian phase approximation.

The position in the mode basis

The MSD needed the integrals ||(\int x\,u_n\,dx||). They are the first row of a matrix that every later chapter uses: the position written in the mode basis, ||[B_{nm} = \int u_n(x)\;x\;u_m(x)\,dx ,||]with ||(x||) measured from the centre of the pore. Like the eigenvalues ||(\lambda_n||), it depends only on the geometry. It answers: if magnetization sits in mode ||(m||) and is multiplied by ||(x||), how much ends up in mode ||(n||)? A linear gradient multiplies the magnetization by exactly such a field, so in Chapter 2 ||(\mathbf B||) is how the gradient couples the modes. ||(\Lambda||) and ||(\mathbf B||) together are everything a pore contributes to the signal.

• (b) About the centre, ||(x - L/2||) is odd and ||(\cos(n\pi x/L)||) has parity ||((-1)^n||). The integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval is zero.
  • (c, d) ||(\cos a\cos b = \frac12[\cos(a-b) + \cos(a+b)]||), and for ||(k \neq 0||), ||(\int_0^L (x - \tfrac L2)\cos\frac{k\pi x}{L}\,dx = \frac{L^2}{(k\pi)^2}\big[(-1)^k - 1\big]||) (integrate by parts).

(a) ⇒ The modes are real and ||(B_{nm} = \int u_n\,x\,u_m\,dx||) is unchanged when ||(n||) and ||(m||) swap. (b) ⇒ Put ||(y = x - L/2||). Then ||(u_n||) has parity ||((-1)^n||) in ||(y||), and ||(y||) is odd, so ||(u_n\,y\,u_m||) has parity ||((-1)^{n+m+1}||). For ||(n + m||) even it is odd, and its integral over ||([-L/2, L/2]||) is zero. → In particular the diagonal vanishes: a mode is never coupled to itself. (c) ⇒ ||(B_{0n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt L}\sqrt{\frac 2L}\int_0^L(x - \tfrac L2)\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx = \frac{\sqrt2}{L}\cdot\frac{L^2[(-1)^n-1]}{(n\pi)^2} = -\frac{2\sqrt2\,L}{(n\pi)^2}||) for odd ||(n||). ⇒ ||(B_{0n}^2 = \dfrac{8L^2}{(n\pi)^4}||): exactly the weights in the mean-squared displacement of Exercise 4 (there you computed ||(\int x\,u_n||) from a wall; centring only changes ||(n = 0||)). data.text/markdown:
Beyond the mean-squared displacement: cumulants of the displacement

The MSD is one number per time. The propagator holds the whole distribution of displacements ||(X = x - x_0||), averaged over where the spins start: ||[\bar P(X,t) = \frac{1}{V}\iint \delta\big(X - (x - x_0)\big)\,P(x\,|\,x_0,t)\,dx\,dx_0 .||]A compact way to describe a distribution is by its cumulants ||(\kappa_n||): the mean (||(\kappa_1||), zero here by symmetry), the variance (||(\kappa_2 = \langle X^2\rangle||)), and then the shape (||(\kappa_4 = \langle X^4\rangle - 3\langle X^2\rangle^2||) for a symmetric distribution). In 1D define ||[D(t) = \frac{\langle X^2\rangle}{2t},\qquad K(t) = \frac{\kappa_4}{\kappa_2^2} = \frac{\langle X^4\rangle}{\langle X^2\rangle^2} - 3 .||]||(D(t)||) is the apparent diffusivity of the figure above. ||(K(t)||), the excess kurtosis, measures how far the shape is from a Gaussian. Free diffusion is Gaussian at every time, so ||(K = 0||): any nonzero ||(K||) comes from the geometry. The cumulants are the Taylor coefficients of the logarithm of the characteristic function: ||[\ln\big\langle e^{iqX}\big\rangle = \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(iq)^n}{n!}\,\kappa_n = -\frac{q^2}{2}\langle X^2\rangle + \frac{q^4}{24}\,\kappa_4 - \dots||]Keep this line in mind. Chapter 3 shows that two very short gradient pulses measure exactly ||(\langle e^{iqX}\rangle||), so in that limit ||(D(t)||) and ||(K(t)||) are what diffusion and kurtosis imaging estimate. Chapter 2 shows what changes when the pulses are not short.

data.text/html: ⇒ Shift the coordinate to the slab centre, ||(y = x - L/2||), so that odd powers average to zero. The displacement is ||(X = y - y_0||). ⇒ Expand: ||(\langle X^2\rangle = 2\langle y^2\rangle - 2\langle y\,y_0\rangle||) and ||(\langle X^4\rangle = 2\langle y^4\rangle - 8\langle y^3y_0\rangle + 6\langle y^2y_0^2\rangle||) (using ||(\langle y^3y_0\rangle = \langle y\,y_0^3\rangle||), because ||(P||) is symmetric in ||(x||) and ||(x_0||)). ⇒ Each mixed average is a mode sum, as in Exercise 4: ||(\langle f(y)\,g(y_0)\rangle = \frac1L\sum_n e^{-D\lambda_n t}\,f_n\,g_n||), with ||(f_n = \int f\,u_n\,dx||). ⇒ The coefficients of ||(y||), ||(y^2||), ||(y^3||) follow from integrating by parts. With ||(k_n = n\pi/L||): ||[y_n = -\frac{2\sqrt2\,L^{3/2}}{(n\pi)^2}\ (n\ \text{odd}),\qquad (y^2)_n = \frac{2\sqrt2\,L^{5/2}}{(n\pi)^2}\ (n\ \text{even} \ge 2),\qquad (y^3)_n = \sqrt2\,L^{7/2}\Big[-\frac{3}{2(n\pi)^2} + \frac{12}{(n\pi)^4}\Big]\ (n\ \text{odd}),||]and zero otherwise; for ||(n=0||) only ||((y^2)_0 = L^{5/2}/12||) survives. → ||(D(t)/D||) and ||(K(t)||) depend on ||(t||) only through ||(Dt/L^2||): one curve for all slabs.

Show that \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(X = x - x_0||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e then has a \u003cstrong\u003etriangular\u003c/strong\u003e distribution on \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||([-L, L]||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e, and that its excess kurtosis is \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(K_\\infty = -3/5||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e.\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(b)\u003c/strong\u003e Show that its characteristic function is \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\langle e^{iqX}\\rangle = \\operatorname{sinc}^2(qL/2)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e, with \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\operatorname{sinc}z = \\sin z/z||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. Expand \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\ln\\operatorname{sinc}^2(qL/2)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e to order \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(q^4||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e and read off \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\kappa_2||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e and \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\kappa_4||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. Do they agree with (a)?\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(c)\u003c/strong\u003e In the figure \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(K(t)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e is \u003cstrong\u003epositive\u003c/strong\u003e at short times before it turns negative. Explain both signs.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

• (a) The density of a sum of two independent variables is the convolution of their densities: two boxes give a triangle. For the moments use symmetry, ||(\langle X^4\rangle = 2\int_0^L X^4\,\frac{L - X}{L^2}\,dX||).
  • (b) The characteristic function of a sum of independent variables is the product of theirs. You need ||(\ln\operatorname{sinc}z = -z^2/6 - z^4/180 - \dots||)
  • (c) Split the spins into two groups: those far from both walls, and those within about ||(\sqrt{Dt}||) of one.

(a) ⇒ ||(x||) and ||(x_0||) are independent and uniform on ||([0, L]||), so ||(X||) has the convolution of two boxes of height ||(1/L||): ||[\bar P(X) = \frac{L - |X|}{L^2},\qquad |X|\le L .||]⇒ ||(\langle X^2\rangle = \frac{2}{L^2}\int_0^L X^2(L - X)\,dX = \frac{2}{L^2}\Big(\frac{L^4}{3} - \frac{L^4}{4}\Big) = \frac{L^2}{6}||), the long-time MSD of Exercise 4. ✓ ⇒ ||(\langle X^4\rangle = \frac{2}{L^2}\Big(\frac{L^6}{5} - \frac{L^6}{6}\Big) = \frac{L^4}{15}||). ⇒ ||(K_\infty = \dfrac{L^4/15}{L^4/36} - 3 = \dfrac{12}{5} - 3 = -\dfrac35||). → Negative: compared with a Gaussian of the same variance, the triangle has a broad shoulder and no tails at all. Every bounded distribution leans this way. (b) ⇒ ||(\langle e^{iqX}\rangle = \langle e^{iqx}\rangle\,\langle e^{-iqx_0}\rangle = \big|\langle e^{iqx}\rangle\big|^2||), and ||(\langle e^{iqx}\rangle = \frac1L\int_0^L e^{iqx}dx = e^{iqL/2}\operatorname{sinc}(qL/2)||). So ||(\langle e^{iqX}\rangle = \operatorname{sinc}^2(qL/2)||). ⇒ With ||(z = qL/2||): ||(\ln\operatorname{sinc}^2z = -\frac{z^2}{3} - \frac{z^4}{90} - \dots = -\frac{q^2L^2}{12} - \frac{q^4L^4}{1440} - \dots||) ⇒ Compare with ||(-\frac{q^2}{2}\kappa_2 + \frac{q^4}{24}\kappa_4||): ||(\kappa_2 = L^2/6||) and ||(\kappa_4 = -L^4/60||), so ||(K = \kappa_4/\kappa_2^2 = -36/60 = -3/5||). ✓ (c) ⇒ Short times. Most spins are far from the walls and diffuse freely, with variance ||(2Dt||). Spins within about ||(\sqrt{Dt}||) of a wall are held back and spread less. A mixture of zero-mean Gaussians with different variances ||(\sigma^2||) has ||(K = 3\,\mathrm{Var}(\sigma^2)/\langle\sigma^2\rangle^2 > 0||): a sharper peak and heavier tails than one Gaussian. The hindered fraction is about ||((S/V)\sqrt{Dt}||), so ||(K||) grows like ||(\sqrt t||) at first, just as ||(D(t)||) first drops like ||(\sqrt t||) (Mitra et al. 1992). ⇒ Long times. Every spin feels both walls, and the bounded triangle of (a) takes over: ||(K\to-3/5||). → In between, ||(K||) peaks at about ||(+0.2||) near ||(Dt \approx 0.03\,L^2||) and crosses zero near ||(Dt \approx 0.08\,L^2||). The same geometry gives both signs: a kurtosis measured at one diffusion time cannot tell heterogeneity from restriction on its own.

Other geometries

The recipe is always the same: solve ||(-\nabla^2 u = \lambda u||) with ||(\partial u/\partial n = 0||) on the walls. In a disk or sphere, separate in polar or spherical coordinates. The radial part becomes a Bessel function, and the wall condition picks out the roots ||(\alpha||) of its derivative.

data.text/markdown:
A surface instead of a volume: cylindrical surfaces and concentric layers

Water trapped between the wraps of myelin moves along thin sheets. Canales-Rodríguez, Tax et al. (2025) model each sheet as the surface of a cylinder of radius ||(r||), and the myelin sheath as a stack of impermeable concentric cylinders separated by very thin layers of water. Along the axis the motion is free. Across it, a spin moves on a circle. Modes on the circle. With arc length ||(s = r\phi||), the eigenproblem is ||(-u'' = \lambda u||) with ||(u||) periodic: a circle has no wall, so periodicity replaces the wall condition. ||[u_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi r}},\qquad u_n = \frac{\cos n\phi}{\sqrt{\pi r}},\ \frac{\sin n\phi}{\sqrt{\pi r}},\qquad \lambda_n = \frac{n^2}{r^2}\quad(n\ge1,\ \text{each twice}).||]The slowest decay time is ||(\tau_1 = r^2/D||), about 3.4 times longer than for the inside of a disk of the same radius (||(0.295\,R^2/D||)): a spin on the rim cannot cut across, it has to go around. Concentric layers. The walls between layers are impermeable, so the modes of the whole sheath are simply the modes of each circle, and every layer keeps its own uniform mode (the ||(\kappa = 0||) case of the next section). A uniform start puts in layer ||(i||) a share of spins proportional to its circumference: ||[E = \sum_i w_i\,E(r_i),\qquad w_i = \frac{r_i}{\sum_j r_j}.||]The layers are evenly spaced between the inner radius (the axon) and the outer radius; in the 2025 simulations they are 7.5 nm apart, roughly a 4–5 nm lipid bilayer plus about 3 nm of water. Outer layers count more, so a single-cylinder fit returns an effective radius biased towards the outer radius. The 2025 paper approximates it by the radius-weighted mean ||(\sum_i w_i r_i = \sum_i r_i^2/\sum_i r_i||). Canales-Rodríguez, Tax et al. (2026) (arXiv 2603.23421) then derived the exact PGSE signal for one cylindrical surface from exactly these modes, with the matrix method of Chapter 2. They name distributions of concentric radii as a natural extension. → A layer of finite thickness is an annulus between two radii. Its modes combine the Bessel functions ||(J_m||) and ||(Y_m||), with the wall condition at both radii; the cylindrical surface is the limit of a very thin annulus.

(a) ⇒ ||(\lambda<0||): ||(\cosh||) and ||(\sinh||) are not periodic, so no solutions. ⇒ ||(\lambda = 0||): ||(u = A + Bs||) is periodic only if ||(B = 0||): the uniform mode. ⇒ ||(\lambda = k^2 > 0||): ||(u = A\cos ks + B\sin ks||). Periodicity, ||(u(s+2\pi r) = u(s)||), needs ||(2\pi r k = 2\pi n||), so ||(k = n/r||) and ||(\lambda_n = n^2/r^2||). Both ||(\cos||) and ||(\sin||) survive: each eigenvalue appears twice (unlike the slab, where the wall condition removed the sine). ⇒ Normalise: ||(\int_0^{2\pi r}\cos^2(ns/r)\,ds = \pi r||) and ||(\int_0^{2\pi r}1\,ds = 2\pi r||), so ||(u_0 = 1/\sqrt{2\pi r}||) and ||(u_n = \cos(n\phi)/\sqrt{\pi r}||), ||(\sin(n\phi)/\sqrt{\pi r}||). (b) ⇒ The number of spins in a layer is density × area, and the area of a cylindrical surface of length ||(\ell||) is ||(2\pi r_i\ell||). With equal density and length, layer ||(i||) holds a fraction ||(2\pi r_i\ell/\sum_j 2\pi r_j\ell = r_i/\sum_j r_j||). ⇒ The layers do not exchange spins, so the total signal is the weighted sum of the layer signals. (c) ⇒ Surface: ||(\tau_1 = r^2/D = 1/0.8 = 1.25||) ms. In the long-time limit the variance of ||(x||) is ||(r^2/2||) on the surface and ||(R^2/4||) inside the cylinder, so the surface also looks larger. Both effects make myelin water distinguishable from intra-axonal water, in principle.

data.text/markdown:
When the interfaces are not reflecting

Everything so far assumed impermeable walls. The recipe for the eigenmodes stays the same, ||(-\nabla^2u = \lambda u||), but the condition at the interfaces changes, and with it the modes:
  • Permeable membranes. The compartments are no longer separate problems. The eigenmodes belong to the whole domain: each mode spans both sides of a membrane, with a continuous flux and a jump in value set by ||(\kappa||). With ||(\kappa = 0||) every compartment has its own uniform mode (||(\lambda = 0||) once per compartment). Opening the membrane turns all but one of these into slowly decaying exchange modes. Their rate is the exchange rate between compartments, the basis of the Kärger (1985) model (Chapter 3).
  • Relaxing walls. The lowest eigenvalue is no longer zero. Even the most uniform mode fades: magnetization is lost at the walls. For weak relaxivity its rate is ||(D\lambda_0 \approx \varrho\,S/V||), the surface-to-volume ratio times the relaxivity (Brownstein & Tarr 1979).
  • Perfect sinks. All modes vanish at the wall, and the slowest one fades with ||(\lambda_0 = (\pi/L)^2||) in a slab: nothing survives.
  • Periodic boundaries. The modes become ||(\cos(2\pi n x/L)||) and ||(\sin(2\pi n x/L)||), each eigenvalue appearing twice. The uniform mode survives: nothing is lost, it just leaves on one side and re-enters on the other.
The modes remain orthonormal in all these cases, so everything in the previous sections (projection, propagator, time scales) carries over unchanged. Try it in a slab of ||(L = 8||) µm with ||(D = 2||) µm²/ms, a membrane in the middle, and a choice of outer walls. The modes are computed numerically (a fine grid with the interface rules built in), so you can compare them with the formulas of the next exercise.

data.text/markdown:
1b · The Bloch–Torrey equation and the expected value of the phase

From Bloch to Bloch–Torrey

After the 90° pulse the magnetization lies in the transverse plane. Write it as one complex number, ||(m = M_x + iM_y||). In the frame rotating at the Larmor frequency, the only field left is the diffusion gradient's, ||(\mathbf g(t)\cdot\mathbf r||). A spin at ||(\mathbf r||) therefore precesses at angular frequency ||(\gamma\,\mathbf g(t)\cdot\mathbf r||), which on its own gives ||(\partial m/\partial t = -i\gamma\,\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf r\, m||). The spins also diffuse, and magnetization is carried with them exactly like the concentration in 1a. Torrey (1956) added the two effects to Bloch's (1946) equations: ||[\boxed{\ \frac{\partial m}{\partial t} = D\,\nabla^2 m \;-\; i\gamma\,\mathbf g(t)\cdot\mathbf r\; m\ }\qquad m(\mathbf r,0) = \rho,\qquad \frac{\partial m}{\partial n}=0 \text{ on impermeable interfaces}.||]
  • Diffusion smooths phase differences out; the gradient winds them up. Every regime in this course is a contest between those two.
  • The 180° pulse of the spin echo (Hahn 1950) flips the sign of all phase gathered so far. We account for it by using the effective gradient, whose sign flips at each 180° pulse.
  • The scanner measures the sum over the voxel: ||(S(T) = \int_\Omega m(\mathbf r,T)\,d\mathbf r||), and we report ||(E = S/S_0||).
  • The domain, interface and boundary conditions are the same as in 1a. So the geometry enters exactly as before: through the eigenmodes. The gradient adds a coupling between them (Chapter 2).

The full problem every simulator solves

The magnetization lives in the same compartments, with the same conditions, as the concentration in 1a. Two things are added: the gradient, and relaxation, which can differ between compartments. With the gradient written as ||(\mathbf g(t) = f(t)\,\mathbf g||) (for PGSE, ||(f = +1||) during the first lobe and ||(-1||) during the second, once the 180° pulse is folded in), each compartment obeys ||[\frac{\partial m_n}{\partial t} = \nabla\cdot(D_n\nabla m_n) - \frac{m_n}{T_{2,n}} - i\gamma f(t)\,(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf r)\,m_n\ \text{ in }\Omega_n,\qquad m_n(\mathbf r,0) = \rho_n,||]
Where Condition Meaning
outer boundary ||(\Gamma_n||) ||(D_n\,\partial m_n/\partial n = 0||) (or periodic, with the phase of 1a) no spins leave the simulated block
membrane ||(\Gamma_{nm}||) ||(D_n\,\partial m_n/\partial n_n = -D_m\,\partial m_m/\partial n_m||) what leaves one side enters the other
membrane ||(\Gamma_{nm}||) ||(D_n\,\partial m_n/\partial n_n = \kappa_{nm}\big(c_{nm}m_m - c_{mn}m_n\big)||) the flux is driven by the jump across the membrane
and the signal is ||(S(T) = \int_\Omega m(\mathbf r, T)\,d\mathbf r||), ||(E = S/S_0||). The simulators of Chapters 4 and 5 solve this problem as it stands. The exact methods of Chapter 2 and the formulas of Chapter 3 simplify it in three steps: ① Uniform ||(T_2||): relaxation then multiplies the signal by ||(e^{-T/T_2}||), which cancels in ||(E||) (Exercise 10). Drop the ||(T_2||) term. ② Equal densities: ||(c_{nm} = 1||); with ||(\rho = 1||) the start is ||(m = 1||). ③ One compartment: impermeable interfaces, so each pore is solved on its own. This is the boxed equation above. → Each step is a statement about the tissue, and each can be false: compartments do relax differently (Exercise 10), and membranes do leak. Chapters 4 and 5 are how to find out what a simplification costs.

data.text/markdown:
The same problem in weak form

The Bloch–Torrey equation makes a demand at every point: both sides must be equal everywhere in ||(\Omega||). The same problem can be stated as a demand on averages instead. That second statement, the weak form, is where most numerical methods start, and it shows how the boundary conditions enter them. ⇒ Write the equation as residual ||(= 0||) (one compartment for now): ||(\ \partial_tm - \nabla\cdot(D\nabla m) + i\gamma f(t)\,(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf r)\,m = 0||). ⇒ Multiply by an arbitrary test function ||(w(\mathbf r)||) and integrate over ||(\Omega||). If the result is zero for every ||(w||), the residual itself must be zero. ⇒ Integrate the diffusion term by parts (Green's identity). Half of the derivatives move onto ||(w||), and a boundary term appears: ||[\int_\Omega w\,\partial_tm\,d\mathbf r + \int_\Omega D\,\nabla w\cdot\nabla m\,d\mathbf r + i\gamma f(t)\int_\Omega w\,(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf r)\,m\,d\mathbf r = \oint_{\partial\Omega}w\,D\,\frac{\partial m}{\partial n}\,dS\qquad\text{for every } w .||]This is the weak form. It needs only first derivatives of ||(m||), so ||(m||) may have kinks, which the equation itself would not allow. ⇒ The boundary term holds the wall conditions. Length scales: who wins, diffusion, the gradient or the walls?

Bloch–Torrey contains a handful of lengths. Which regime you are in, and so which approximation or simulation method works, depends on which length is the shortest.
Length Formula What it measures
Pore size ||(L||) (slab width) or ||(R||) (radius) where the walls are
Diffusion length ||(\ell_D = \sqrt{DT}||) how far a spin wanders during the experiment
Phase length ||(\ell_q = 1/(\gamma g T)||) (or ||(1/q||) for pulses) over which distance the gradient has wound one radian of phase
Gradient (dephasing) length ||(\ell_g = \left(D/\gamma g\right)^{1/3}||) the distance over which diffusion and dephasing balance
Surface-relaxation length ||(\ell_\varrho = D/\varrho||) how far a spin travels along a relaxing wall before it loses its magnetization
||(T_2||) diffusion length ||(\sqrt{D\,T_2}||) how far a spin travels before bulk ||(T_2||) relaxation has removed it
Grebenkov (2007) lists the first four as ||(L||), ||(L_p = \sqrt{DT}||), ||(L_q||) and the relaxation length ||(L_h = D/\varrho||). The gradient length ||(\ell_g||) is the one that sets the strong-gradient regime (Stoller, Happer & Dyson 1991; de Swiet & Sen 1994). The three are not independent: ||(\ell_g^3 = \ell_D^2\,\ell_q||).
Shortest length Regime What the signal does
||(\ell_D||) free diffusion, or short times ||(E \approx e^{-bD}||); walls only add a correction ||(\propto (S/V)\sqrt{DT}||)
||(L||) motional narrowing (fully restricted) spins average over the pore; slab: ||(\ln E \approx -\gamma^2g^2L^4T/(120D)||) (Robertson 1966)
||(\ell_g||) localisation magnetization survives only in layers of thickness ||(\sim\ell_g||) at the walls; ||(\ln E \propto -DT/\ell_g^2 \propto -g^{2/3}T||), not ||(-g^2||)
For relaxing walls compare ||(\ell_\varrho||) with ||(L||). If ||(\ell_\varrho \gg L||) (the usual case in tissue), spins visit the walls many times before relaxing: the loss is uniform, at rate ||(\varrho\,S/V||) (the fast-diffusion regime, Brownstein & Tarr 1979). If ||(\ell_\varrho \ll L||), relaxation is limited by how fast spins reach the wall.

data.text/markdown:
Two pictures of the same signal

Field picture. Solve the Bloch–Torrey equation for ||(m(\mathbf r,t)||) everywhere, then integrate at the echo. Chapters 2 to 4 work this way. Path picture. Follow single spins. Each spin random-walks along its own path ||(\mathbf r(t)||) (reflected at walls) and gathers its own phase ||[\varphi = \gamma\int_0^T \mathbf g(t)\cdot\mathbf r(t)\,dt .||]The voxel contains so many spins that the signal is the average phase factor over all possible paths, starting from uniformly spread positions: ||[E = \big\langle e^{-i\varphi}\big\rangle_{\text{paths}} .||]In the language of probability: the signal is the characteristic function of the random phase. Chapter 5 (Monte Carlo) works this way. Sign convention: some texts write ||(e^{+i\varphi}||). For a refocused echo the two give the same magnitude. The two pictures give exactly the same ||(E||). This is an example of the Feynman–Kac relation between parabolic PDEs and averages over random paths. Carr & Purcell (1954) already computed echo attenuation this way, as an average phase over random walks; the general relation is due to Kac (1949), inspired by Feynman's (1948) path integrals. You can derive it yourself in a few lines.

For a smooth ||(f||), put ||(y = x-s||): ||[\int p(x-y) f(y)\,dy = \int p(s)\Big[f(x) - s f'(x) + \tfrac{s^2}{2}f''(x) - \dots\Big]ds = f(x) + D\,\delta t\, f''(x) + O(\delta t^2),||]because ||(p||) integrates to 1, has mean 0 and variance ||(2D\,\delta t||) (higher moments are of order ||(\delta t^2||)). ⇒ The phase. ||(e^{-i\gamma g y\delta t} = 1 - i\gamma g y\,\delta t + O(\delta t^2)||). ⇒ Apply the step rule to ||(f(y) = (1 - i\gamma g y\,\delta t)\,w(y,t)||) and keep terms up to first order in ||(\delta t||): ||[w(x,t+\delta t) = w(x,t) + D\,\delta t\,\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2} - i\gamma g(t)\,x\,\delta t\; w(x,t) + O(\delta t^2).||]⇒ Move ||(w(x,t)||) to the left, divide by ||(\delta t||) and let ||(\delta t\to 0||): ||[\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} = D\,\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2} - i\gamma\, g(t)\,x\, w .||]This is the Bloch–Torrey equation. ✓ (d) ⇒ Initial: at ||(t=0||) every walker has zero phase and the walkers are spread uniformly, so ||(w(x,0) = \rho = 1/L||), the same as ||(m(x,0)||). ⇒ Walls: reflected walkers are never lost, so no weighted walkers flow through a wall: ||(\partial w/\partial x = 0||), the Neumann condition on ||(m||). ⇒ Same equation, same initial and interface conditions, so the same solution: ||(w = m||). Then (a) gives ||[\int m(x,T)\,dx = \big\langle e^{-i\varphi}\big\rangle .\qquad\blacksquare||]→ What it means. The magnetization at ||(x||) is the phase-weighted density of spins at ||(x||). The PDE tracks the density; the random walk tracks the spins. → What it means for simulation. Step (b), repeated many times, is a recipe: move each walker with a Gaussian step, then add its phase. That is a Monte Carlo simulation (Chapter 5). Written in the eigenbasis of 1a, the same alternation of "diffuse, then add phase" is the multiple propagator method (Chapter 2). Both converge to the Bloch–Torrey solution as ||(\delta t\to0||), for exactly the reason shown in (c).

Chapter 2 · Series expansions: two ways to expand the signal Two different series, often confused.
